stages.title: Atoms and molecules
stages.hook: If you kept cutting a piece of copper wire in half again and again, would you ever reach a smallest piece? What would it be?
explain: Everything around you is made of atoms. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope. Each kind of atom has its own name, such as hydrogen, oxygen or carbon.

Atoms often join together in groups. A group of atoms joined together is a molecule. Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom make a water molecule. Some things, like a piece of iron, are just huge numbers of the same atom side by side.
Atoms are not used up when things change. In a burning candle or a melting ice cube the atoms are rearranged, not destroyed. This idea is the heart of chemistry.

example.q: A water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. How many atoms are in 3 water molecules?
steps: Count atoms in one molecule: 2 + 1 = 3.
Multiply by the number of molecules: 3 × 3.

analogies.home: Atoms are like Lego bricks. A few bricks snap together to make a small model, a molecule.
analogies.city: Think of a city as made of bricks. Atoms are the bricks of everything, from a bus to a tree.
analogies.music: A few notes make a chord. A few atoms make a molecule.
analogies.nature: A sand beach is made of countless grains. An object is made of countless atoms.

stages.title: Elements and the periodic table
stages.hook: There are about 118 known elements. How could you organise them so a new learner can find any one quickly?
explain: An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. Gold, oxygen, iron and carbon are elements. Each has a symbol, such as Au for gold, O for oxygen, Fe for iron and C for carbon.

The periodic table lists all the elements in order of atomic number, which is the number of protons in each atom. It is laid out in rows called periods and columns called groups. Elements in the same group behave in a similar way.
Most elements are metals, on the left and centre. Non-metals are on the right. The group of very unreactive gases on the far right are the noble gases, such as helium and neon.

example.q: Sodium (Na) and potassium (K) are in the same group. What can you predict?
steps: Elements in the same group have similar behaviour.
Sodium is a soft, reactive metal.
So potassium is probably a soft, reactive metal too.
example.a: Potassium is also a soft, reactive metal

analogies.home: A shelf of books sorted by topic helps you find one fast. The table sorts elements.

analogies.sport: A league table ranks teams, and the periodic table orders elements by atomic number.

stages.title: Compounds and mixtures
stages.hook: Salt on your chips and sand on a beach: one is a compound and one is a mixture. What is the difference?
explain: A compound is made when atoms of different elements join together by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Its properties are very different from those of hydrogen and oxygen gas.
A mixture is made of different substances that are only mixed, not joined. Air and sea water are mixtures. The parts keep their own properties and can often be separated by physical means.
Compounds can only be split by chemical reactions. Mixtures can be split by sieving, filtering or evaporating, and they can contain parts in any amount.

example.q: Is salt water a compound or a mixture?
steps: Salt is dissolved in water, not chemically joined.
It can be separated by evaporating the water.
The amounts of salt and water can vary.

stages.title: Chemical symbols and formulas
stages.hook: H₂O means water, but what would H₂O₂ mean? Why does a tiny number change everything?
explain: Each element has a symbol of one or two letters. The first letter is capital and the second is small, like C for carbon and Cl for chlorine. A formula uses symbols and small numbers to show a substance. The small number, called a subscript, tells how many atoms of that element are in one unit.

H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. If there is no number, it means 1. CO₂ has 1 carbon and 2 oxygen atoms. NaCl has 1 sodium and 1 chlorine. A number written in front, like 3H₂O, means three separate molecules.
Changing a subscript makes a different substance. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, which is not safe to drink, while H₂O is water.

steps: Ca has no number, so 1 calcium.

stages.title: Chemical bonding basics
stages.hook: Salt is hard and crunchy but water is runny. If both are just atoms joined together, why are they so different?
explain: A chemical bond is the force that holds atoms together. Atoms bond because they become more stable when they do. There are three common kinds: ionic, covalent and metallic.

In covalent bonding, atoms share pairs of electrons. This is common between non-metal atoms and makes molecules like water and carbon dioxide. In ionic bonding, a metal atom gives electrons to a non-metal atom. This makes charged atoms called ions, and opposite charges attract. Sodium chloride is ionic.
In metallic bonding, the outer electrons of metal atoms move freely, which is why metals carry electricity and can be bent into shape.

example.q: Sodium (a metal) bonds with chlorine (a non-metal). Which bond type is likely?
steps: Metal plus non-metal usually means electrons are transferred.

stages.title: Chemical reactions
stages.hook: A nail left in damp air turns orange-brown. Is this the same kind of change as ice melting?
explain: In a chemical reaction, substances called reactants change into new substances called products. The atoms are rearranged: bonds in the reactants break and new bonds form. The products have different properties from the reactants.

Signs of a reaction include a colour change, bubbles of gas, a new solid forming, heat or light given out, and a new smell. Rusting, burning, baking and rotting are all reactions. Melting and dissolving are physical changes.
The total mass does not change in a closed system. This is the law of conservation of mass. We write word equations such as: hydrogen + oxygen → water.

steps: Reactants: magnesium and oxygen.
Product: magnesium oxide.

stages.title: Acids, bases and pH
stages.hook: Lemon juice tastes sour and soap feels slippery. Is there a number that tells us how acidic something is?
explain: Acids taste sour, like lemon juice and vinegar. Bases, also called alkalis when dissolved in water, feel soapy, like soap and baking soda solution. Never taste unknown chemicals; in science we use indicators to test instead.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral (pure water) and above 7 is alkaline. Each step on the scale is a factor of ten in acidity, so pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.

Indicators such as litmus paper and universal indicator change colour with pH. When an acid and a base react, they neutralise each other and make a salt and water. This is why some indigestion tablets work.

example.q: A liquid turns blue litmus red. Is it an acid or an alkali?

So the liquid is an acid, with pH below 7.

stages.title: States of matter and phase changes
stages.hook: Why does a puddle disappear on a warm day even though it never reaches boiling point?
explain: Matter can be solid, liquid or gas. In a solid the particles vibrate in fixed places. In a liquid they move past each other. In a gas they are far apart and move fast in all directions. Adding heat gives the particles more energy.

Melting is solid to liquid, freezing is liquid to solid, boiling or evaporating is liquid to gas, condensing is gas to liquid, and sublimation is solid straight to gas. Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure.

During a change of state the temperature stays steady while the energy is breaking the forces between particles. Evaporation can happen below the boiling point, from the surface only, which is how puddles dry.

example.q: Ice at 0 °C is heated. The temperature stays at 0 °C while it melts. Why?
steps: The heat energy is used to loosen the bonds between water molecules.
So it does not raise the temperature.
Once all melted, the temperature rises again.
example.a: The energy goes into changing state, not raising temperature

stages.title: Density, solubility and concentration
stages.hook: A giant log floats but a tiny pebble sinks. What property decides whether something floats?
explain: Density tells how much mass is packed into a given volume: density = mass ÷ volume. It is often measured in g/cm³. Water has density about 1 g/cm³. Things less dense than water float on it, and denser things sink.

Solubility is how much of a substance can dissolve in a given amount of water. A solution is made of a solute (the dissolved stuff) and a solvent (the liquid doing the dissolving). When no more can dissolve, the solution is saturated. Warmer water usually dissolves more solid.

Concentration says how much solute is in a volume of solution. For example, 10 g of salt in 1 litre of solution is 10 g per litre. More solute in the same volume means a stronger, more concentrated solution.

example.q: A block has a mass of 60 g and volume of 20 cm³. What is its density? Will it float in water (1 g/cm³)?
steps: Density = mass ÷ volume = 60 ÷ 20.
3 is more than 1, so it sinks.
